title: Breaking Through With The Jobava London! | The Sensei Speedrun | GM Naroditsky

moves.spoken: Against a strong opponent, reach for something you're comfortable in — the Jobava London: Nc3 with Bf4, still effective at this level and not deeply known.
Black has several sound replies to Bf4 — c5, the symmetrical Bf5, e6, g6, a6 — and a6 is a sensible one, taking the Nb5 leap off the table.
moves.teaches: In the Jobava, a6 pre-empts White's key Nb5 jump.

moves.spoken: We answer with the pedestrian e3, and note Black still has Bf5 or c5 available.
Rather than the g4 sideline, we keep it strictly positional and start with Bd3.
After Bd6 we face a choice, and one option is out: Bxd6 is bad because cxd6 hands Black a broad central pawn mass. Bg3 is the usual retreat.
moves.teaches: Don't trade into a recapture that gifts your opponent a central pawn majority.

moves.spoken: But there's nothing to fear if Black takes on f4 — after exf4 the doubled f-pawns actually increase our central control. Think of it as a reverse Maroczy bind, clamping the e5 square.
moves.teaches: Doubled f-pawns from an exf4 recapture bind e5 and boost central control — welcome them, don't avoid them.

moves.spoken: Both sides castle and often maneuver around the two bishops staring each other down; Black's ...Bxf4 with a timely c5 is a fine equalizer that strikes at the bind.
Now the heart of London and Jobava play: plant the Pillsbury knight on e5. It's a superb piece in its own right, and it clears a path for the other pieces to join an attack.
moves.teaches: The e5 knight is the London's engine — a dominant outpost that opens lines for the heavy pieces.

moves.spoken: The maneuver to know: Qf3, then swing to h3 to bear down on h7. The pawn is guarded by the f6-knight, but that knight is far from invulnerable — and from g3 the queen can x-ray instead.
moves.teaches: Route the queen f3-h3 to pressure h7; then look for ways to remove its knight defender.
